transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that regular aerobic exercise can significantly improve memory and cognitive function in older adults, according to researchers at the University of British Columbia. The study followed 120 adults aged 60 to 80 over a six-month period. Half the participants did aerobic exercise like walking, cycling, or swimming three times a week, while the other half did only stretching and toning exercises. At the end of the study, the aerobic exercise group showed significant improvements in memory and executive function compared to the stretching group. Brain scans also showed increased blood flow to the hippocampus, the part of the brain responsible for memory. Researchers say that exercise is one of the best ways to maintain brain health as we age and may help reduce the risk of dementia and Alzheimer's disease.

2. What part of the brain showed increased blood flow?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: Stockholm has announced an ambitious plan to become the world's first carbon-neutral capital city by 2030. The Swedish capital, which already has one of the lowest per capita carbon emissions among major European cities, plans to achieve this goal through a combination of measures including transitioning all public transportation to electric vehicles, increasing the use of renewable energy, improving energy efficiency in buildings, and expanding cycling infrastructure. The city also plans to plant more trees and create more green spaces to absorb carbon dioxide. City officials say that while the goal is ambitious, it is achievable with the right policies and investments. Stockholm's plan is being watched closely by other cities around the world as a model for how major urban centers can address climate change.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Researchers at Harvard University have developed a tiny, insect-sized robot that can walk, climb, and fly, inspired by the biology of real insects. The robot, which weighs less than a gram, uses tiny artificial muscles made of piezoelectric materials that contract when electricity is applied. Unlike larger drones, these micro-robots can navigate tight spaces and are resilient enough to keep flying even after colliding with obstacles. Researchers say that these tiny robots could have many applications, including search and rescue operations in collapsed buildings, pollinating crops, inspecting machinery in hard-to-reach places, and even exploring other planets. The technology is still in the early stages, but researchers are working on making the robots more autonomous and capable of carrying small payloads like sensors or cameras.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Sarah): Hey Jake, how's the cooking going? I remember you were learning to make roasted chicken a while back.
Man (Jake): Oh, it's going great! I've been cooking a lot more since then. I actually really enjoy it now.
Woman: That's awesome! I'm so glad to hear it. What have you been making?

Man: Well, I've mastered roasted chicken, of course. And I've been making a lot of pasta dishes, stir-fries, and even some soups. Last week I tried making chili for the first time, and it turned out really good.
Woman: Wow, you've been busy! How's your cholesterol? Has it improved?
Man: Yeah, actually! I went back to the doctor last month, and she said my cholesterol has come down a lot. She was really impressed. She said I should keep doing what I'm doing.
Woman: That's fantastic! Cooking at home really makes a difference, doesn't it?
Man: It really does. And I've found that I actually enjoy cooking. It's relaxing, and it feels good to eat something I made myself. Plus, I'm saving money by not eating out as much.
Woman: That's another great benefit. Do you have a favorite thing to make now?

Man: Hmm, I really like making stir-fries because they're quick and you can put almost anything in them. But I also really enjoy making soup on weekends—it's cozy and you can make a big batch and eat it all week.
Woman: Soups are great for meal prep. Have you tried baking yet?

Man: Not really. Baking seems more precise and scientific, and I'm a little intimidated by it. Cooking is more forgiving—you can just add a little more of this or that. But baking requires exact measurements, right?

Woman: Yeah, baking is more precise. But it's not that hard once you get the hang of it. I could teach you some basics if you want. We could make something simple like chocolate chip cookies or banana bread.
Man: That sounds fun! I'd like that. When are you free?
Woman: How about next Sunday afternoon? I can come over and we can bake together. I'll bring the recipes and some of the ingredients.
Man: Perfect! I'm looking forward to it. And thanks again for getting me started on cooking. It's really changed how I eat.
Woman: No problem! I'm just glad you stuck with it. Okay, I'll see you next Sunday.
Man: See you Sunday!

9. What happened to Jake's cholesterol?

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The history of video games is a story of rapid technological innovation and cultural transformation. From simple arcade games to immersive virtual reality experiences, video games have evolved enormously over the past 50 years, becoming one of the largest and most influential forms of entertainment in the world.

The first commercially successful video game was Pong, released by Atari in 1972. Pong was a simple table tennis simulation with two paddles and a ball, but it was a huge hit and helped launch the video game industry. The 1970s saw the rise of arcade games, with classics like Space Invaders, Pac-Man, and Donkey Kong becoming cultural phenomena.

In the late 1970s and early 1980s, home video game consoles began to appear. The Atari 2600, released in 1977, was one of the first successful home consoles, allowing people to play arcade-style games in their living rooms. But the video game industry crashed in 1983 due to market saturation and poor-quality games, and many companies went out of business.

The industry was revived in 1985 when Nintendo released the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) in North America. The NES came with the game Super Mario Bros., which became one of the best-selling games of all time. Nintendo dominated the home console market for several years, with iconic games like The Legend of Zelda and Metroid.

The 1990s saw the rise of 16-bit consoles like the Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis, and the beginning of the 3D revolution with the Sony PlayStation and Nintendo 64. Games became more complex and visually impressive, with 3D graphics and CD-quality audio. The PlayStation introduced many adult-oriented games, expanding the demographic of video game players beyond children.

The 2000s saw the rise of online gaming, with consoles like the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 connecting players around the world. The Nintendo Wii introduced motion controls, bringing gaming to a wider, more casual audience. And the rise of smartphones in the late 2000s created a massive new market for mobile games.

Today, the video game industry is bigger than the movie and music industries combined. Games are played by billions of people around the world, on everything from consoles and PCs to smartphones and virtual reality headsets. And with advances in technology like cloud gaming and artificial intelligence, the future of video games looks more exciting than ever.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Sleep is essential for our physical and mental health, yet many people don't get enough of it. While we often think of sleep as a passive activity where the body simply rests, research has shown that the brain is actually very active during sleep, performing important functions that are crucial for our well-being.

One of the most important functions of sleep is memory consolidation. During sleep, especially during deep sleep and REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep, the brain processes and consolidates memories from the day, transferring information from short-term to long-term memory. This is why getting a good night's sleep before an exam is so important—your brain needs sleep to remember what you've studied.

Sleep also plays a crucial role in physical health. During sleep, the body repairs cells, releases hormones that regulate growth and appetite, and strengthens the immune system. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to a wide range of health problems, including obesity, diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, and a weakened immune system. People who don't get enough sleep are also more likely to have accidents and make mistakes.

Mental health is also closely tied to sleep. Sleep deprivation can cause irritability, mood swings, anxiety, and difficulty concentrating. Long-term sleep problems are associated with an increased risk of depression and other mental health disorders. And it works both way—mental health problems can also cause sleep problems, creating a vicious cycle.

So how much sleep do we need? The recommended amount varies by age. Adults should aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep per night, teenagers need 8 to 10 hours, and children need even more. But many people get significantly less than this, often because of work schedules, stress, or the use of electronic devices before bed.

There are many things you can do to improve your sleep quality. Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day helps regulate your body's internal clock. Avoiding caffeine and alcohol before bed, creating a comfortable sleep environment, and limiting screen time before bed can all help. Regular exercise can also improve sleep, though it's best not to exercise too close to bedtime.
Sleep is not a luxury—it's a biological necessity. Prioritizing sleep is one of the best things you can do for your health and well-being.

21. How much sleep should adults get per night?

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: The ancient Olympic Games were one of the most important cultural and sporting events of the ancient world. Held in honor of the Greek god Zeus, the games took place every four years at Olympia, a sacred site in southern Greece, for nearly 12 centuries. The ancient Olympics were much more than just a sporting event—they were a religious festival, a cultural celebration, and a symbol of Greek unity.

The first recorded Olympic Games took place in 776 BCE, though the games may have existed even earlier. According to legend, the games were founded by the hero Heracles (Hercules in Roman mythology) as a way to honor his father Zeus. The games were so important to the Greeks that a truce was called during the games, allowing athletes and spectators to travel safely to Olympia even during times of war.

Only free Greek men were allowed to compete in the ancient Olympics—women, slaves, and foreigners were excluded. Married women weren't even allowed to attend the games as spectators, on penalty of death. The athletes competed in the nude, which was a sign of their status as free men and was also believed to showcase the beauty of the human body.

The ancient Olympics featured a variety of events, many of which are still part of the modern games. The most prestigious event was the stadion, a short sprint of about 180 meters. Other events included longer races, wrestling, boxing, the pentathlon (which included running, jumping, discus, javelin, and wrestling), and chariot racing. Unlike the modern games, there were no silver or bronze medals—only the winner of each event received a prize, which was a simple olive wreath called a kotinos.

Winning an Olympic event was one of the highest honors a Greek man could achieve. Victors were celebrated as heroes in their home cities, and they often received financial rewards, free meals for life, and other privileges. Poets wrote odes in their honor, and statues were erected in their likeness.

The ancient Olympic Games came to an end in 393 CE, when the Roman emperor Theodosius I, a Christian, banned all pagan festivals, including the Olympics. The games were revived nearly 1,500 years later, in 1896, when the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece. The modern Olympics have grown into the world's largest sporting event, with athletes from over 200 countries competing. While the modern games are very different from the ancient ones in many ways, they still carry on the spirit of competition, excellence, and international friendship that the ancient Greeks began.
